general_conventions: M1 = method mark; a later A1 that depends on it cannot be scored without it; in 'show that' items the final A mark is often A0 (the given value earns nothing on its own).
C1 = compensatory method mark, awarded automatically if the final answer is correct; A1 = accuracy mark for the final value; B1 = independent mark for a stated fact or step.

ECF (error carried forward): later numerical parts can earn full credit if consistent with an earlier wrong answer; ECF is allowed after arithmetic (AE), transcription (TE) and power-of-ten (POT) errors but not after wrong physics / wrong equation (XP).
POT: power-of-ten slip (usually an SI-prefix conversion) loses the mark where it occurs, then ECF applies.

SF: giving more significant figures than justified is not penalised; too few is dealt with in individual guidance (often 1 SF is allowed where stated); the SF penalty is applied only once in the paper unless a question explicitly demands a given number of SF.
XP: use of an incorrect equation counts as wrong physics even if it happens to give the right number.
CON: a contradiction within the same response cancels the mark; BOD = benefit of doubt; ^ marks an omission (not wrong but incomplete).

Notation: '/' separates alternatives; Reject/Not = not creditworthy; Ignore = irrelevant extra; Allow = acceptable; words in brackets are not essential; underlined words must be present; AW = alternative wording; ORA = or reverse argument.
General rule for Section B: substitution into an equation may be made with any quantity as subject unless the guidance says otherwise.
Significant figures: if data are given to 2 SF allow answers to 2 or more SF; fewer than 2 SF penalised once only in the whole paper unless guidance says otherwise.
B marks are independent; M marks must be seen and A marks depend on them; C marks can be credited implicitly from correct later working.
MCQ: two responses for a single-answer question score zero; contradictory responses score zero.

Level-of-response guidance (generic): level set by science content using best fit; higher/lower mark within level depends on the italicised communication statement. No LoR question on this paper (the MS template sentence naming the LoR questions was left unfilled as 'X and Y').

pitfalls: Equilibrium forces act on the same body so cannot be an N3 pair; body may move at constant velocity.

questions.context: Force constant from force–extension graph (extension in mm).

questions.topic: 1.1 Practical skills assessed in a written examination
questions.context: Describe how to determine cross-sectional area of a copper wire.
questions.answer: Micrometer measures diameter at several places, average, then A = πd^2/4.
marking_points: B1: micrometer (or callipers) to measure diameter
B1: measure at several places/orientations and average
B1: A = πr^2 with r = d/2 (or πd^2/4)
pitfalls: Using a ruler; forgetting to halve diameter.

questions.context: Show E = kL/A from definitions.
questions.answer: E = (F/A)/(x/L) with F = kx gives kL/A.
marking_points: M1: E = stress/strain, F = kx, σ = F/A, ε = x/L
A1: clear substitution to E = kL/A

questions.context: Calculate E and its percentage uncertainty from k, L, A with uncertainties.
pitfalls: Multiplying percentages instead of adding.

questions.context: Decide if a researched E = 1.17 × 10^11 N m^-2 is consistent with the result.
marking_points: M1: quantitative comparison e.g. % difference = 2.6% or uncertainty range
A1: difference within uncertainty so consistent
allow_reject_ignore: Allow other quantitative comparisons e.g. range 1.11–1.19 using 1.15 or 1.16–1.24 using 1.2.
ECF from (c)(ii) uncertainty; 1.7% using 3 SF value allowed.
pitfalls: Saying 'close' without a quantitative comparison.

questions.context: Explain how molecule motion produces compressions and rarefactions.
questions.answer: Molecules oscillate parallel to energy transfer, creating regions of high and low pressure/density.
marking_points: B1: oscillation parallel to direction of energy transfer/wave
B1: regions of higher and lower pressure / molecules closer together and further apart
allow_reject_ignore: Allow particles; allow high/low concentration or density.
pitfalls: Implying molecules travel with the wave.

questions.context: Explain formation of a stationary wave with nodes and antinodes between speaker and reflector.
questions.answer: Incident and reflected waves superpose; in phase gives antinodes, antiphase gives nodes.
marking_points: B1: incident and reflected waves interfere/superpose
B1: constructive (in phase) gives maximum amplitude/antinodes
pitfalls: Not mentioning that the two waves travel in opposite directions/reflection.

questions.context: Explain why nodes are not zero and get closer to zero near the reflector.
questions.answer: Wave amplitude decreases with distance (and on reflection), so reflected and incident amplitudes differ; cancellation incomplete; difference grows further from A.
marking_points: B1: wave intensity/amplitude decreases with distance (or energy absorbed at plate)
B1: reflected wave amplitude less than incident (or incomplete destructive interference)
B1: amplitude difference increases with distance from A (ORA)
pitfalls: Not linking unequal amplitudes to incomplete cancellation.

questions.subtopic: speed of sound from node spacing
questions.context: Speed of sound from node separation 0.84 m at 200 Hz.
pitfalls: Using λ = 0.84 m (node spacing is λ/2).

questions.topic: 1.1 Practical skills assessed in a written examination
questions.context: Suggest improvement to reduce uncertainty in speed of sound.
questions.answer: Measure across several node spacings (or lower f / repeat and average).
marking_points: B1: one of: measure across several minima; use lower frequency (longer λ); repeat and take mean

questions.context: Work done on an electron accelerated through 3.0 V.
Explain need for minimum frequency for photoemission.
questions.answer: Photon energy ∝ f; electron released only if one photon's energy ≥ work function.
marking_points: B1: emission only if photon energy ≥ work function
pitfalls: Using wave/intensity arguments; describing energy accumulation over time.

questions.context: Explain why ammeter reading is proportional to radiation intensity.
questions.answer: Intensity ∝ photon arrival rate; one photon releases one electron; current = rate of charge flow.
marking_points: B1: intensity proportional to rate of incident photons (above threshold)
B1: current = charge flow per unit time so ∝ emission rate

questions.context: Intensity from photon frequency, electron emission rate and plate area.
pitfalls: Forgetting to divide by area; treating electron rate and photon rate differently.

questions.topic: 3.5 Newton's laws of motion and momentum
questions.context: Average force on a 0.058 kg ball reversing from 7.2 to 3.6 m/s in 52 ms.
pitfalls: Subtracting speeds instead of accounting for reversal of direction.

questions.context: Show the rebounding ball lands within the 15 cm-radius ring centred 2.0 m away.
marking_points: C1: target range 1.85–2.15 m (or 9 cm from centre)
A1: 2.09 lies in range / 9 cm < 15 cm
allow_reject_ignore: C1 can be implied by the A1 statement.
pitfalls: Using incoming speed 7.2 m/s; no explicit comparison with ring radius.

questions.topic: 1.1 Practical skills assessed in a written examination
questions.context: Use table data to justify video camera over stopwatch.
questions.answer: Intervals of 0.1 s are comparable with reaction time (~0.2 s); video can be replayed/frame-by-frame with smaller uncertainty.
marking_points: B1: time intervals small / particle fast (relative to reaction time)
B1: video has finer resolution / stopwatch uncertainty large due to reaction time
pitfalls: Vague 'more accurate' without reference to data/reaction time.

questions.topic: 1.1 Practical skills assessed in a written examination
questions.context: One other precaution for accurate terminal velocity.
questions.answer: Avoid parallax e.g. camera level with and perpendicular to scale.
marking_points: B1: method to avoid parallax errors

questions.context: Show from distance–time data the terminal velocity is about 0.3 m/s.
questions.answer: Constant 2.7 cm per 0.1 s gives 0.27 m/s.
marking_points: M1: v = s/t with data from 0.2 s onwards giving 0.27 m/s
A1: second calculation showing speed constant (terminal velocity reached)
allow_reject_ignore: Allow justification that distance per interval stays the same.
pitfalls: Using total distance/total time including acceleration phase.

questions.context: Use the terminal velocity formula to find particle diameter and classify soil.
allow_reject_ignore: Allow v = 0.3 m/s (r = 0.52 mm, d ≈ 1.0 mm).
Allow computing v at the class boundaries and showing 0.27 m/s lies in sand's range.
pitfalls: Comparing radius with a diameter table; mm/m conversion.
